new_statements.quote: Tunen is a tonal language and tones play an important role in marking both lexical and grammatical contrasts. There are three tone levels on the surface: H, L, and downstepped H (↓H, realised phonetically at a mid height). The tonal system is best analysed as having two tones underlyingly, H (high) and L (low). [...] [p.83:] Loanwords from languages with stress seem to be adopted in Tunen with H tone on the stressed syllable and low tone elsewhere, e.g. simíti 'cement', hɛbanána 'banana', ikísin 'kitchen'.
new_statements.citation: Kerr, Elisabeth J. 2024. Tunen syntax and information structure. PhD dissertation, Leiden University (LOT Dissertation Series 676). Amsterdam: LOT.
new_statements.locator: sec. 4.2.6.1 'Tone inventory', pp.77-78 (pdf p.99); loanword remark sec. 4.2.7, p.83 (pdf p.105)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (LOT 676, 28.4 MB, text layer; alongside) opened. Sec. 4.2.6.1 'Tone inventory' begins at the foot of printed p.77 (pdf p.99) and continues on p.78: 'Tunen is a tonal language and tones play an important role in marking both lexical and grammatical contrasts. There are three tone levels on the surface: H, L, and downstepped H (↓ H, realised phonetically at a mid height). The tonal system is best analysed as having two tones underlyingly, H (high) and L (low).' -- verbatim as quoted (only a space in '↓ H' differs). It continues: TBU = syllable following Janssens 1988 and Mous 2003, tonal minimal pairs, contour tones, H tone spread one TBU rightward, utterance-final tone lowering, downdr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tunen is described purely as a two-level (H/L, with downstep and H-tone spread) terraced tone language whose tone-bearing unit is the syllable; the source assigns no word stress or accent to native words and treats stress only as a property of donor languages, mapped onto H tone in loans. No location of word stress is stated anywhere in the accessible descriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal processes noted: H tone spread one syllable rightward, downstep from floating L, utterance-final tone lowering and vowel reduction (Kerr 2024 sec. 4.2.4, 4.2.6.2-4.2.6.4; Boyd 2015 p.38, both after Mous 2003: 286-287).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical/grammatical tone at word and utterance level; Kerr explicitly says Tunen prosody (beyond tone) was not studied (p.361). Boyd 2015 p.38 and Mous 2014 p.74 fn. independently give the same two-tone characterisation for Nen.
new_statements.identity_note: tune1241 is Glottolog's bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO code [baz] 'Tunen', split in 2012 (ISO 639-3 CR 2011-080, saved) into [tvu] Tunen (tune1261) and [nvo] Nyokon (nyok1243). All descriptions examined (Kerr 2024/2025, Boyd 2015 'Nen', Mous 'Nen', Dugast 'tunen, parler des Banen') describe Tunen proper = tune1261 (Kerr's fieldwork: Ndikiniméki area varieties); Nyokon is covered separately in (Lovestrand 2011, Mous 2022, also tonal with no stress statement). Not to be confused with nenn1238 'Nen' of Papua New Guinea.

sources.note: Sec. 4.2.6.1 (pp.77-78): Tunen is a tonal language, surface H/L/downstepped H, two underlying tones, TBU = syllable. Sec. 4.2.7 (p.83): loanwords from stress languages are adopted with H tone on the source-language stressed syllable and L elsewhere. No statement on native word stress/accent; p.361 says Tunen prosody was 'not studied in great detail'.
